VIDEO.title: Matthew 11:1-19 – Jesus vs. John the Baptist Disagreement EXPLAINED
VIDEO.series: The Gospel of Matthew Every Word (playlist of 58 videos)

hand: Blessed is he who does not take offense at Me.
SUMMARY: The teacher reads Matthew 11:1-19. John, in prison, sends his disciples to ask Jesus, 'Are You the One who is to come, or shall we look for someone else?' Jesus points to His works and adds a beatitude: 'blessed is he who does not take offense at Me.' Then He praises John to the crowds as more than a prophet, the messenger of Malachi 3:1 and the Elijah who was to come, and compares 'this generation' to children in the marketplace.

The video's bold claim: John got Jesus wrong. John had preached that judgment was near: the axe at the root, the winnowing fork in hand (3:10-12). Jesus did none of that; He taught a kingdom that grows slowly, like a mustard seed and leaven (13:31-33). If John held the Essenes' view of an imminent, fiery end, the delay would puzzle him. Jesus taught that the old age and the new overlap for a time (12:32; Mark 10:30; Luke 18:30).

Jesus answers with evidence, stringing together Isaiah 26:19, 29:18-19, 35:5-6 and 61:1. Each of those passages also speaks of judgment, but Jesus stops short of it. He does not mention release for captives, which John in prison might have hoped for. Then: 'blessed is he who does not take offense at Me' (11:6), trust Me even when what I do does not make sense yet.

Jesus defends John before the crowds. Verses 10-14 form a chiasm: John is the messenger (11:10) and John is Elijah (11:14) are the bookends; at the center, 11:12: 'the kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and violent men take it by force.' With D. A. Carson, the teacher reads it as the kingdom forcefully advancing while violent men try to plunder it. That explains why John is in prison: where the kingdom advances, some will attack it.

The parable (11:16-19): children in the marketplace call out to their playmates, angry that they won't join the wedding game (flute and dancing) or the funeral game (dirge and mourning). The playmates who won't play are John and Jesus: John fasts and they say 'He has a demon'; Jesus eats with tax collectors and sinners and they call Him a glutton and a drunkard. 'Yet wisdom is vindicated by her deeds.'

The lesson: in order to understand what the Lord is doing, the people have to trust Him first. They trusted their expectations; even John did. Blessed is the one who recognizes that the Lord is not doing what they think He should, and trusts Him anyway.
QUOTES: The bottom line is John expects Jesus to be doing stuff that he's not doing.
Blessed is the one who trusts me even when I do something that doesn't initially make sense.
The parable is not only meant to be interpreted by the listener. What's really going on is the listener is also interpreted by the parable.
In order to understand what the Lord is doing, the people have to trust him first.
God might be doing something right now that is outside the bounds of your own expectations.

method.h: Put the pieces on the table
method.p: The teacher's method: collect the odd details first (an unexpected beatitude, a chiasm with a puzzling center, a parable), lay them out like pieces on a table, then ask what lesson they add up to for the original audience. For a parable, ask who each character stands for and where you fit in the story.

LSB_QUOTES.text: And blessed is he who does not take offense at Me.
And from the days of John the Baptist until now the kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and violent men take it by force.
Yet wisdom is vindicated by her deeds.

src.text: Now when John in prison heard of the works of Christ, he sent word by his disciples and said to Him, “Are You the One who is to come, or shall we look for someone else?”

lines.text: John's disciples had confronted Jesus once before, about fasting (9:14). Now John himself asks. What follows is an in-house disagreement between the Messiah and His baptizer.
Matthew tells later why Herod Antipas had jailed John: John had said his marriage to Herodias was unlawful (14:3-4).

left.text: His winnowing fork is in His hand, and He will thoroughly clear His threshing floor; and He will gather His wheat into the barn, but He will burn up the chaff with unquenchable fire.”

right.text: He spoke another parable to them, “The kingdom of heaven is like leaven, which a woman took and hid in three sata of flour until it was all leavened.”

lines.text: The video: John got it wrong about Jesus. He preached that judgment was so near the axe was already at the root (3:10). Jesus came and did none of that; He taught a kingdom like a mustard seed, wheat and weeds together, and leaven: a slow process.

Some think John was an Essene. If so, he expected an imminent judgment with power and glory through the Messiah: the old age going out with a bang. But the old and new ages overlap for a time ('this age' and 'the age to come': 12:32; Mark 10:30; Luke 18:30).

QUESTION.title: Go and report what you hear and see

src.text: And Jesus answered and said to them, “Go and report to John what you hear and see: the blind receive sight and the lame walk, the lepers are cleansed and the deaf hear, the dead are raised up, and the poor have the gospel preached to them.

left.text: Then the eyes of the blind will be opened, / And the ears of the deaf will be unstopped. Then the lame will leap like a deer, / And the tongue of the mute will shout for joy.

lines.text: Instead of chiding John, Jesus points to objective evidence, stringing together Isaiah 26:19, 29:18-19, 35:5-6 and 61:1.
Each of those Isaiah passages also promises judgment in its immediate context ('your God will come with vengeance,' 35:4), but Jesus stops short of quoting it.
Isaiah 61:1 also promises 'release to captives / And freedom to prisoners.' Jesus does not mention it to John, who is in prison.

QUESTION.title: Blessed is he who does not take offense

src.text: And blessed is he who does not take offense at Me.”

lines.text: This should sound familiar: it is a beatitude, the 'Blessed are…' form that opened the Sermon on the Mount (5:3-12).
Its meaning: blessed is the one who trusts Me even when I do something that doesn't initially make sense. Maybe Jesus is freeing captives, just not in the way that is immediately obvious.
'Take offense' is skandalizō, 'to stumble' or 'fall away' (compare 13:57; 26:31).

ELIJAH.title: A reed shaken by the wind?

src.text: Now as these men were going away, Jesus began to speak to the crowds about John, “What did you go out into the wilderness to see? A reed shaken by the wind? But what did you go out to see? A man dressed in soft clothing? Behold, those who wear soft clothing are in kings’ palaces! But what did you go out to see? A prophet? Yes, I tell you, and one who is more than a prophet.

lines.text: The crowds knew John: he was famous. Watching the two disagree in public, they might start to doubt both. So Jesus defends John: his question did not come from weakness, moral failure, or fear of prison.
Reeds grew along the Jordan where John baptized. Kings' palaces like Herod Antipas's at Tiberias held men in soft clothing; John, in camel's hair, was nothing like the king who jailed him (3:4).

left.text: “Behold, I am going to send My messenger, and he will prepare the way before Me. And the Lord, whom you seek, will suddenly come to His temple; and the messenger of the covenant, in whom you delight, behold, He is coming,” says Yahweh of hosts.

right.text: “Behold, I am going to send an angel before you to keep you along the way and to bring you into the place which I have prepared.

lines.text: Jesus quotes Malachi 3:1 and probably alludes to Exodus 23:20 to link John to Elijah, whom Malachi promises 'before the coming of the great and awesome day of Yahweh' (Malachi 4:5).
In Malachi it is 'before Me' (God); in Matthew 'ahead of You': the Lord who comes is Jesus.

src.text: And from the days of John the Baptist until now the kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and violent men take it by force.

lines.text: This verse has sent translators in different directions. The teacher sides with D. A. Carson: the kingdom is not passively suffering violence but forcefully advancing, while violent or rapacious men try to plunder it.

Because it sits at the center of the chiasm, it is what Jesus wants hearers to focus on. Imprisonment is not unexpected; it is part of the kingdom advancing. Jesus is explaining why John is in jail, and showing that none of this undermines God's plan, John, or Himself.
Luke's version: 'the good news of the kingdom of God is proclaimed, and everyone is forcing his way into it' (Luke 16:16).

src.text: For all the prophets and the Law prophesied until John. And if you are willing to accept it, John himself is Elijah who was to come. He who has ears to hear, let him hear.

lines.text: Why does Jesus care whether the people, and by extension John, are willing to accept it? Why talk about ears? Maybe the answer is tied to the lesson for them.
John even dressed like Elijah: a leather belt around his waist (3:4; 2 Kings 1:8). Later Jesus says again, 'Elijah already came, and they did not recognize him' (17:12).

src.text: “But to what shall I compare this generation? It is like children sitting in the marketplaces, who call out to the other children, and say, ‘We played the flute for you, and you did not dance; we sang a dirge, and you did not mourn.’

lines.text: Ancient Jewish parables often began, 'A parable: to what may it be compared? It is like…' The force of a parable is felt through the comparison. Listeners step inside the story, find where they fit, and face a crisis of decision.
The children are 'this generation.' They call out critically to their playmates, upset that they will not join their games: a wedding game (flute and dancing) and a funeral game (dirge and mourning).

src.text: For John came neither eating nor drinking, and they say, ‘He has a demon!’ The Son of Man came eating and drinking, and they say, ‘Behold, a gluttonous man and a drunkard, a friend of tax collectors and sinners!’ Yet wisdom is vindicated by her deeds.”

lines.text: Who are the playmates who won't play? John and Jesus. That is why Jesus goes straight to the criticisms of each: John's fasting is called demonic, and Jesus' table fellowship with sinners is called gluttony.
What John and Jesus are doing is the wisdom of God at work, and her deeds prove it right (11:19).
'A glutton and a drunkard' echoes the charge against a rebellious son in Deuteronomy 21:20.
A parable is not only interpreted by the listener; the listener is interpreted by the parable. The crowd had to see themselves among the sulking children.

The teacher cites the scholar Joachim Jeremias (the captions say 'Wim Jeremas') for the sense: you give orders and criticize; you call the Baptist mad because he fasts, and Jesus for eating with tax collectors. You reject both the call to repent and the good news, and play childish games with God's messengers.
Luke ends the parable, 'wisdom is vindicated by all her children' (Luke 7:35): those who received John and Jesus.

TERMS.def: Teaching about the last things: judgment, the age to come. The captions spell it 'esquetology.'

TERMS.term: This age and the age to come
TERMS.def: Jewish way of dividing history; Jesus speaks of both (12:32; Mark 10:30). The video: in Jesus the two overlap for a time.
A strict Jewish group expecting God's imminent judgment; some lived in the wilderness. Whether John was one is debated.
A mirrored pattern (A B C B' A') whose main point sits at the center. The captions spell it 'kayazm.'
A unit of text, such as one story or teaching. The captions say 'paricopy.'
A short story or comparison in which the characters illustrate a lesson, often about how God deals with people.
God's wisdom personified, as in Proverbs 8-9; 'vindicated by her deeds' (11:19).

WORDS.gloss: To come; 'the One who is to come.'
To cause to stumble; passive: take offense, fall away. Look up: BDAG, σκανδαλίζω.
Middle: to press forward forcefully; passive: to suffer violence. Look up: BDAG, βιάζω.
To seize, snatch, take by force.
To beat the breast in mourning.
To justify, vindicate, show to be right.

BACKGROUND.p: Herod the Great's hilltop fortress east of the Dead Sea, in Antipas's territory of Perea. Josephus says John was sent there in bonds and put to death (Antiquities 18.5.2).
Children in ancient towns played at grown-up events: weddings with pipes and dancing, funerals with wailing and beating the breast. Refusing to play either one was a familiar childish quarrel.

Josephus, Philo and Pliny describe the Essenes; many link them to the Qumran community near the Dead Sea. John's wilderness life and message of judgment have led some to suggest a connection, but the Gospels never call him an Essene.
Malachi 4:5 promised Elijah before the day of Yahweh. Jews still pour a cup for Elijah at the Passover meal. Jesus says John fulfilled that role 'if you are willing to accept it.'

WITNESSES.text: Whence it is evident, that neither did he send as being himself in doubt, nor did he ask in ignorance.
WITNESSES.src: Homilies on Matthew 36, on 11:3. Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, series 1, vol. 10 (public domain).

WITNESSES.text: For both of them received one ministry, and both of them became forerunners.

DEBATES.p: The video: yes; John's expectations of judgment were wrong. Chrysostom: no; John asked for his disciples' sake, 'neither did he send as being himself in doubt.' Others: a real but faithful question from a prisoner. Jesus answers kindly and then praises John.

DEBATES.h: Violence against the kingdom, or the kingdom advancing?
DEBATES.p: The Greek verb in 11:12 can be read as passive ('suffers violence') or middle ('forcefully advances'). Some read 'violent men' as opponents like Herod; others as eager people pressing in (compare Luke 16:16). Chrysostom took it as stirring hearers to earnestness.

Possible but unproven. John lived in the wilderness and preached imminent judgment, like the Qumran community, but he called all Israel to repent and baptized once, unlike the Essenes' repeated washings.

CAREFUL_INTRO: Small slips worth knowing (offered gently; the video's main points stand):
CAREFUL: Isaiah 61:1 holds both phrases: 'To bring good news to the afflicted' and 'To proclaim release to captives.' The video says Jesus quotes 'the verse right before'; it is the same verse.
The Greek of 11:12 can be read as middle ('forcefully advances') or passive ('suffers violence'). The reading the video takes from D. A. Carson is the middle, not the 'active voice.'
The word for the children 'calling out' (prosphōneō) simply means to call out to someone; the critical tone comes from the context, not the word itself.

The summary of the parable is credited to Joachim Jeremias (captions: 'Wim Jeremas'); the wording could not be checked here. Lepers being cleansed is not in the Isaiah passages Jesus draws on; that sign stands on its own (compare 2 Kings 5).
That John was an Essene is a guess, not a fact; the Gospels never say so.

QUESTIONS: Have you ever expected God to act one way and been surprised? What did you do with that?
Read Isaiah 35:4-6 and 61:1-2. What did Jesus leave out when answering John, and why might that matter?
What does 'blessed is he who does not take offense at Me' ask of you this week?
How do you read 11:12: the kingdom under attack, or the kingdom advancing? What difference does it make?
In the parable, are you ever one of the children who want God to play your game?
Where might God be working right now outside the bounds of your expectations?
APPLICATION_VIDEO: Put the pieces together: an unexpected beatitude ('blessed is he who does not take offense at Me'), a chiasm whose center says the kingdom advances and is attacked, and a parable of children who sulk because John and Jesus will not play their games. The lesson for the original audience: in order to understand what the Lord is doing, the people have to trust Him first. They did not trust Jesus; they trusted their expectations and preconceived notions about Him. Even the best of them, John the Baptist, fell into confusion. Jesus gives this beatitude for that moment: blessed is the one who recognizes that the Lord is not doing what they think He should, and trusts Him anyway. That still speaks today: God might be doing something right now that is outside the bounds of your own expectations. What are you going to do about it?
APPLICATION_ADDED: Study note (added): write down one place where God is not doing what you expected (a prayer, a plan, a relationship). Next to it, write Matthew 11:6, and one 'report' of what you have seen Him do, as Jesus told John's disciples to report what they heard and saw.

# Matthew 11:1-19 Study Notes: Matthew 11:1-19 – Jesus vs. John the Baptist Disagreement EXPLAINED
Video: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8M0B_bqDAUQ
Channel: Every Word | Length: 28:05 | Series: The Gospel of Matthew Every Word (playlist of 58 videos)
Series hub: https://shea-nelson.github.io/workout-app/bible/

Translation: Legacy Standard Bible (LSB). The video reads from another English translation; quotations here are LSB. Notes marked [Background] are added study helps, not from the video.

## Summary (from the video)
- The teacher reads Matthew 11:1-19. John, in prison, sends his disciples to ask Jesus, 'Are You the One who is to come, or shall we look for someone else?' Jesus points to His works and adds a beatitude: 'blessed is he who does not take offense at Me.' Then He praises John to the crowds as more than a prophet, the messenger of Malachi 3:1 and the Elijah who was to come, and compares 'this generation' to children in the marketplace.
- The video's bold claim: John got Jesus wrong. John had preached that judgment was near: the axe at the root, the winnowing fork in hand (3:10-12). Jesus did none of that; He taught a kingdom that grows slowly, like a mustard seed and leaven (13:31-33). If John held the Essenes' view of an imminent, fiery end, the delay would puzzle him. Jesus taught that the old age and the new overlap for a time (12:32; Mark 10:30; Luke 18:30).
- Jesus answers with evidence, stringing together Isaiah 26:19, 29:18-19, 35:5-6 and 61:1. Each of those passages also speaks of judgment, but Jesus stops short of it. He does not mention release for captives, which John in prison might have hoped for. Then: 'blessed is he who does not take offense at Me' (11:6), trust Me even when what I do does not make sense yet.
- Jesus defends John before the crowds. Verses 10-14 form a chiasm: John is the messenger (11:10) and John is Elijah (11:14) are the bookends; at the center, 11:12: 'the kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and violent men take it by force.' With D. A. Carson, the teacher reads it as the kingdom forcefully advancing while violent men try to plunder it. That explains why John is in prison: where the kingdom advances, some will attack it.
- The parable (11:16-19): children in the marketplace call out to their playmates, angry that they won't join the wedding game (flute and dancing) or the funeral game (dirge and mourning). The playmates who won't play are John and Jesus: John fasts and they say 'He has a demon'; Jesus eats with tax collectors and sinners and they call Him a glutton and a drunkard. 'Yet wisdom is vindicated by her deeds.'
- The lesson: in order to understand what the Lord is doing, the people have to trust Him first. They trusted their expectations; even John did. Blessed is the one who recognizes that the Lord is not doing what they think He should, and trusts Him anyway.

### Put the pieces on the table
The teacher's method: collect the odd details first (an unexpected beatitude, a chiasm with a puzzling center, a parable), lay them out like pieces on a table, then ask what lesson they add up to for the original audience. For a parable, ask who each character stands for and where you fit in the story.

## Are You the One?
1. John in prison · Matthew 11:2-3: Are You the One?
   Question Matthew 11:2-3: "Now when John in prison heard of the works of Christ, he sent word by his disciples and said to Him, “Are You the One who is to come, or shall we look for someone else?”" https://read.lsbible.org/?q=Matthew+11:2-3
   (video) John's disciples had confronted Jesus once before, about fasting (9:14). Now John himself asks. What follows is an in-house disagreement between the Messiah and His baptizer. (Matthew 9:14)
   [Background] Matthew tells later why Herod Antipas had jailed John: John had said his marriage to Herodias was unlawful (14:3-4). (Matthew 14:3-4)
2. What John expected · Matthew 3:10-12: The axe at the root
   John (Matthew 3:12, LSB): "His winnowing fork is in His hand, and He will thoroughly clear His threshing floor; and He will gather His wheat into the barn, but He will burn up the chaff with unquenchable fire.”"
   Jesus (Matthew 13:33, LSB): "He spoke another parable to them, “The kingdom of heaven is like leaven, which a woman took and hid in three sata of flour until it was all leavened.”"
   (video) The video: John got it wrong about Jesus. He preached that judgment was so near the axe was already at the root (3:10). Jesus came and did none of that; He taught a kingdom like a mustard seed, wheat and weeds together, and leaven: a slow process. (Matthew 3:10; Matthew 13:24-33)
   (video) Some think John was an Essene. If so, he expected an imminent judgment with power and glory through the Messiah: the old age going out with a bang. But the old and new ages overlap for a time ('this age' and 'the age to come': 12:32; Mark 10:30; Luke 18:30). (Matthew 12:32; Mark 10:30)
3. Jesus' answer · Matthew 11:4-5: Go and report what you hear and see
   Isaiah (Isaiah 35:5-6, LSB): "Then the eyes of the blind will be opened, / And the ears of the deaf will be unstopped. Then the lame will leap like a deer, / And the tongue of the mute will shout for joy."
   Evidence Matthew 11:4-5: "And Jesus answered and said to them, “Go and report to John what you hear and see: the blind receive sight and the lame walk, the lepers are cleansed and the deaf hear, the dead are raised up, and the poor have the gospel preached to them." https://read.lsbible.org/?q=Matthew+11:4-5
   (video) Instead of chiding John, Jesus points to objective evidence, stringing together Isaiah 26:19, 29:18-19, 35:5-6 and 61:1. (Isaiah 26:19; Isaiah 29:18-19; Isaiah 61:1)
   (video) Each of those Isaiah passages also promises judgment in its immediate context ('your God will come with vengeance,' 35:4), but Jesus stops short of quoting it. (Isaiah 35:4)
   [Background] Isaiah 61:1 also promises 'release to captives / And freedom to prisoners.' Jesus does not mention it to John, who is in prison. (Isaiah 61:1-2)
4. A beatitude · Matthew 11:6: Blessed is he who does not take offense
   Trust Matthew 11:6: "And blessed is he who does not take offense at Me.”" https://read.lsbible.org/?q=Matthew+11:6
   (video) This should sound familiar: it is a beatitude, the 'Blessed are…' form that opened the Sermon on the Mount (5:3-12). (Matthew 5:3)
   (video) Its meaning: blessed is the one who trusts Me even when I do something that doesn't initially make sense. Maybe Jesus is freeing captives, just not in the way that is immediately obvious.
   [Background] 'Take offense' is skandalizō, 'to stumble' or 'fall away' (compare 13:57; 26:31).

## More than a prophet

The video's chiasm: A and A' name John's role from Malachi; B and B' place John at the turn of the ages; C is the center.
1. Matthew 11:7-9: A reed shaken by the wind?
   Not weak Matthew 11:7-9: "Now as these men were going away, Jesus began to speak to the crowds about John, “What did you go out into the wilderness to see? A reed shaken by the wind? But what did you go out to see? A man dressed in soft clothing? Behold, those who wear soft clothing are in kings’ palaces! But what did you go out to see? A prophet? Yes, I tell you, and one who is more than a prophet." https://read.lsbible.org/?q=Matthew+11:7-9
   (video) The crowds knew John: he was famous. Watching the two disagree in public, they might start to doubt both. So Jesus defends John: his question did not come from weakness, moral failure, or fear of prison.
   [Background] Reeds grew along the Jordan where John baptized. Kings' palaces like Herod Antipas's at Tiberias held men in soft clothing; John, in camel's hair, was nothing like the king who jailed him (3:4).
2. Malachi 3:1 · Matthew 11:10: Behold, I send My messenger
   Malachi (Malachi 3:1, LSB): "“Behold, I am going to send My messenger, and he will prepare the way before Me. And the Lord, whom you seek, will suddenly come to His temple; and the messenger of the covenant, in whom you delight, behold, He is coming,” says Yahweh of hosts."
   Moses (Exodus 23:20, LSB): "“Behold, I am going to send an angel before you to keep you along the way and to bring you into the place which I have prepared."
   (video) Jesus quotes Malachi 3:1 and probably alludes to Exodus 23:20 to link John to Elijah, whom Malachi promises 'before the coming of the great and awesome day of Yahweh' (Malachi 4:5). (Malachi 4:5)
   [Background] In Malachi it is 'before Me' (God); in Matthew 'ahead of You': the Lord who comes is Jesus.
3. The center · Matthew 11:12: The kingdom suffers violence
   Center Matthew 11:12: "And from the days of John the Baptist until now the kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and violent men take it by force." https://read.lsbible.org/?q=Matthew+11:12
   (video) This verse has sent translators in different directions. The teacher sides with D. A. Carson: the kingdom is not passively suffering violence but forcefully advancing, while violent or rapacious men try to plunder it.
   (video) Because it sits at the center of the chiasm, it is what Jesus wants hearers to focus on. Imprisonment is not unexpected; it is part of the kingdom advancing. Jesus is explaining why John is in jail, and showing that none of this undermines God's plan, John, or Himself.
   [Background] Luke's version: 'the good news of the kingdom of God is proclaimed, and everyone is forcing his way into it' (Luke 16:16). (Luke 16:16)
4. Matthew 11:13-15: John himself is Elijah
   Elijah Matthew 11:13-15: "For all the prophets and the Law prophesied until John. And if you are willing to accept it, John himself is Elijah who was to come. He who has ears to hear, let him hear." https://read.lsbible.org/?q=Matthew+11:13-15
   (video) Why does Jesus care whether the people, and by extension John, are willing to accept it? Why talk about ears? Maybe the answer is tied to the lesson for them.
   [Background] John even dressed like Elijah: a leather belt around his waist (3:4; 2 Kings 1:8). Later Jesus says again, 'Elijah already came, and they did not recognize him' (17:12). (2 Kings 1:8; Matthew 17:10-13)

## Children in the marketplace
1. The parable · Matthew 11:16-17: Children in the marketplace
   Parable Matthew 11:16-17: "“But to what shall I compare this generation? It is like children sitting in the marketplaces, who call out to the other children, and say, ‘We played the flute for you, and you did not dance; we sang a dirge, and you did not mourn.’" https://read.lsbible.org/?q=Matthew+11:16-17
   (video) Ancient Jewish parables often began, 'A parable: to what may it be compared? It is like…' The force of a parable is felt through the comparison. Listeners step inside the story, find where they fit, and face a crisis of decision.
   (video) The children are 'this generation.' They call out critically to their playmates, upset that they will not join their games: a wedding game (flute and dancing) and a funeral game (dirge and mourning).
2. Matthew 11:18-19: A glutton and a drunkard?
   Playmates Matthew 11:18-19: "For John came neither eating nor drinking, and they say, ‘He has a demon!’ The Son of Man came eating and drinking, and they say, ‘Behold, a gluttonous man and a drunkard, a friend of tax collectors and sinners!’ Yet wisdom is vindicated by her deeds.”" https://read.lsbible.org/?q=Matthew+11:18-19
   (video) Who are the playmates who won't play? John and Jesus. That is why Jesus goes straight to the criticisms of each: John's fasting is called demonic, and Jesus' table fellowship with sinners is called gluttony.
   (video) What John and Jesus are doing is the wisdom of God at work, and her deeds prove it right (11:19).
   [Background] 'A glutton and a drunkard' echoes the charge against a rebellious son in Deuteronomy 21:20. (Deuteronomy 21:20)
3. Who is interpreted?: The parable reads the listener
   (video) A parable is not only interpreted by the listener; the listener is interpreted by the parable. The crowd had to see themselves among the sulking children.
   (video) The teacher cites the scholar Joachim Jeremias (the captions say 'Wim Jeremas') for the sense: you give orders and criticize; you call the Baptist mad because he fasts, and Jesus for eating with tax collectors. You reject both the call to repent and the good news, and play childish games with God's messengers.
   [Background] Luke ends the parable, 'wisdom is vindicated by all her children' (Luke 7:35): those who received John and Jesus. (Luke 7:29-35)

## Key people
- Jesus: Answers John with evidence, adds a beatitude, defends John, and tells the parable of the children. [Background] Luke adds that 'at that very time' He healed many (Luke 7:21).
- John the Baptist: In prison, asks if Jesus is the One. The video: his expectations were wrong. [Background] Josephus says Herod Antipas held and executed John at the fortress of Machaerus (Antiquities 18.5.2).
- John's disciples: Carry John's question to Jesus. [Background] They had asked Jesus about fasting before (9:14), and later bury John (14:12).
- The crowds: Watch a public disagreement; Jesus speaks to them about John. [Background] Many had gone out to the Jordan to be baptized by John (3:5-6).
- Elijah: John is 'Elijah who was to come' (11:14). [Background] Elijah was taken up in a whirlwind (2 Kings 2:11); Malachi 4:5 promised his return.
- This generation: The sulking children who reject both John and Jesus. [Background] Jesus uses 'this generation' for the unbelieving people of His day (12:39-45; 23:36).
- Tax collectors and sinners: Jesus' table companions, the reason for the 'friend of' insult. [Background] Compare 9:10-13, at Matthew's house.

## Places [Background]
- Capernaum: Jesus' base, near where He taught and preached 'in their cities' (11:1).
- Tiberias: Herod Antipas's capital, one of the 'kings' palaces' of 11:8.
- Jordan River (named in the video): The wilderness by the Jordan where crowds went out to see John (3:5-6; 11:7).
- Jerusalem: Many of John's hearers came from Jerusalem and Judea (3:5).

## Key terms
- Eschatology: Teaching about the last things: judgment, the age to come. The captions spell it 'esquetology.'
- This age and the age to come: Jewish way of dividing history; Jesus speaks of both (12:32; Mark 10:30). The video: in Jesus the two overlap for a time.
- Essenes: A strict Jewish group expecting God's imminent judgment; some lived in the wilderness. Whether John was one is debated.
- Beatitude: A 'blessed is' saying, like 5:3-12 and 11:6.
- Chiasm: A mirrored pattern (A B C B' A') whose main point sits at the center. The captions spell it 'kayazm.'
- Pericope: A unit of text, such as one story or teaching. The captions say 'paricopy.'
- Parable: A short story or comparison in which the characters illustrate a lesson, often about how God deals with people.
- Wisdom: God's wisdom personified, as in Proverbs 8-9; 'vindicated by her deeds' (11:19). [Background]

## Historical and cultural background [Background: established]
- Machaerus: Herod the Great's hilltop fortress east of the Dead Sea, in Antipas's territory of Perea. Josephus says John was sent there in bonds and put to death (Antiquities 18.5.2).
- Children's games: Children in ancient towns played at grown-up events: weddings with pipes and dancing, funerals with wailing and beating the breast. Refusing to play either one was a familiar childish quarrel.
- Essenes: Josephus, Philo and Pliny describe the Essenes; many link them to the Qumran community near the Dead Sea. John's wilderness life and message of judgment have led some to suggest a connection, but the Gospels never call him an Essene.
- Elijah expected: Malachi 4:5 promised Elijah before the day of Yahweh. Jews still pour a cup for Elijah at the Passover meal. Jesus says John fulfilled that role 'if you are willing to accept it.'

- John Chrysostom (c. AD 390): "For both of them received one ministry, and both of them became forerunners." Homilies on Matthew 37, on 11:14 (John and Elijah). NPNF 1.10 (public domain).
- John Chrysostom (c. AD 390): "Is fasting a good thing, and to be admired? You should then have obeyed John, and received him, and believed his sayings." Homilies on Matthew 37, on 11:18-19. NPNF 1.10 (public domain).

## Where scholars differ [Background: debated]
- Did John doubt? The video: yes; John's expectations of judgment were wrong. Chrysostom: no; John asked for his disciples' sake, 'neither did he send as being himself in doubt.' Others: a real but faithful question from a prisoner. Jesus answers kindly and then praises John.
- Violence against the kingdom, or the kingdom advancing? The Greek verb in 11:12 can be read as passive ('suffers violence') or middle ('forcefully advances'). Some read 'violent men' as opponents like Herod; others as eager people pressing in (compare Luke 16:16). Chrysostom took it as stirring hearers to earnestness.
- Was John an Essene? Possible but unproven. John lived in the wilderness and preached imminent judgment, like the Qumran community, but he called all Israel to repent and baptized once, unlike the Essenes' repeated washings.

## Careful reading notes
Small slips worth knowing (offered gently; the video's main points stand):
- Isaiah 61:1 holds both phrases: 'To bring good news to the afflicted' and 'To proclaim release to captives.' The video says Jesus quotes 'the verse right before'; it is the same verse.
- The Greek of 11:12 can be read as middle ('forcefully advances') or passive ('suffers violence'). The reading the video takes from D. A. Carson is the middle, not the 'active voice.'
- The word for the children 'calling out' (prosphōneō) simply means to call out to someone; the critical tone comes from the context, not the word itself.
- The summary of the parable is credited to Joachim Jeremias (captions: 'Wim Jeremas'); the wording could not be checked here. Lepers being cleansed is not in the Isaiah passages Jesus draws on; that sign stands on its own (compare 2 Kings 5).
- That John was an Essene is a guess, not a fact; the Gospels never say so.

## Reflection and discussion questions
1. Have you ever expected God to act one way and been surprised? What did you do with that?
2. Read Isaiah 35:4-6 and 61:1-2. What did Jesus leave out when answering John, and why might that matter?
3. What does 'blessed is he who does not take offense at Me' ask of you this week?
4. How do you read 11:12: the kingdom under attack, or the kingdom advancing? What difference does it make?
5. In the parable, are you ever one of the children who want God to play your game?
6. Where might God be working right now outside the bounds of your expectations?

## Application
- (video) Put the pieces together: an unexpected beatitude ('blessed is he who does not take offense at Me'), a chiasm whose center says the kingdom advances and is attacked, and a parable of children who sulk because John and Jesus will not play their games. The lesson for the original audience: in order to understand what the Lord is doing, the people have to trust Him first. They did not trust Jesus; they trusted their expectations and preconceived notions about Him. Even the best of them, John the Baptist, fell into confusion. Jesus gives this beatitude for that moment: blessed is the one who recognizes that the Lord is not doing what they think He should, and trusts Him anyway. That still speaks today: God might be doing something right now that is outside the bounds of your own expectations. What are you going to do about it?
- Study note (added): write down one place where God is not doing what you expected (a prayer, a plan, a relationship). Next to it, write Matthew 11:6, and one 'report' of what you have seen Him do, as Jesus told John's disciples to report what they heard and saw.
